title: Seven fat cows
hook: the cupbearer finally remembers, and Yusuf reads the king's dream as seven good years and seven hard
carry: the fat years feed the thin

segments.voice: Yesterday: two dreams in a cell, and a prophet who called his cellmates companions. Your line was start with the one. Did you begin with what matters most? Day sixty-five.

Years pass. Yusuf is still in prison, forgotten by the man who promised to mention him. And then the king of Egypt has a dream that won't leave him alone. He tells his court: I saw seven fat cows, and seven lean cows eating them. And seven green ears of grain, and seven others, dry. Tell me what it means. His advisers shrug. Jumbled dreams, they say. We don't interpret nonsense. And standing in the room, the cupbearer, the freed prisoner, suddenly goes pale. The Qur'an says he remembered, after a long time. Send me, he says. I know someone. Today: seven fat cows.
screen: `FORGOTTEN, FOR YEARS.` → `THE KING'S DREAM.` → `THE CUPBEARER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. The cupbearer comes to the cell and says: Yusuf, you truthful one, explain this dream to us. Notice: truthful one. Years later, he still remembers the thing that mattered about Yusuf. And now watch what Yusuf does. He doesn't say, first get me out of here. He doesn't say, you forgot me. He doesn't bargain at all. He answers, and goes further than he was asked. He says: for seven years, farm as you usually do. What you harvest, leave in the ear, on the stalk, except the little you eat. Then seven hard years will come that eat up what you stored, except a little you keep back. Then a year will come when people have rain, and they'll press fruit and oil again. The king asked for a meaning. Yusuf gives him a plan. Save in the good years. Store the grain in the ear, where it keeps. Eat a little, not a lot. And then he adds a year the dream never mentioned, a fifteenth year of relief. That's what a hopeful reader of dreams does: he sees past the famine to the rain. Jews and Christians tell this story too, in Genesis, where Joseph reads Pharaoh's dream in much the same way. And the lesson carries straight into an ordinary life. Good seasons don't last. Hard seasons don't either. The wise thing is to let the fat years feed the thin. And Yusuf, still in his cell, has just given Egypt a way through the hard years without asking for a thing.
screen: `YUSUF, YOU TRUTHFUL ONE.` · `NO BARGAIN, JUST THE ANSWER.` · `LEAVE IT IN THE EAR.` · `A YEAR OF RAIN AFTER.` · then, large: `THE FAT YEARS FEED THE THIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save one thing today for later. Settle, and breathe. Think about what you have plenty of right now. It might be money this week, or energy, or time, or patience, or a friend's goodwill. Whatever season you're in, there's usually something that's fat right now. Choose one small portion to put by. Five dollars into savings. A meal into the freezer. An hour of rest before the busy week. A kind message to someone before you need them. Picture putting it away, in the ear. If you pray, you can give thanks for the plenty. The bell holds the time.
Seven fat cows. The king's dream, and Yusuf's plan: save in the seven good years to live through the seven hard. Today's word.
Your line: the fat years feed the thin. Put one small thing away today for a harder week you can't see yet. Day sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims draw practical wisdom from Yusuf's interpretation, saving and planning in times of plenty, and often cite it in teaching about stewardship and preparing for hardship.

fork.setup: you're Yusuf, forgotten in prison for years. the man who forgot you comes to ask about the king's dream. what do you do?
options: say: get me out first, then I'll tell you.
give the meaning, and a plan for the hard years.
fork.reveal: no bargain, no blame. he gives a plan: farm seven years, store in the ear, eat a little, and after the hard years, a year of rain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange dream about cows.
what it means: seven good years and seven hard ones, and a plan to let the good feed the hard, from a prisoner who asked nothing in return.
what a scholar hears: 12:49 adds a year of relief not in the dream; commentators say Yusuf knew it by revelation, not from the dream itself. "leave it in the ear" keeps grain from spoiling.

sources.ref: Genesis 41 (Joseph and Pharaoh's dream, named as a neighbor)

notes: The index calls him 'the cupbearer'; the Qur'an says 'the one of the two who was saved' (and 12:41 says he will pour wine for his lord). Kept as cupbearer.
'Leave it in the ear, where it keeps': a common explanation that grain stored on the stalk resists spoilage and pests; confirm wording.
The fifteenth year (12:49): commentators say this was knowledge beyond the dream; stated in the trapdoor.
'The king' is the Qur'an's term (al-malik) in the Yusuf story; not called Pharaoh.
